content: Great to hear this is happening, although it would have been nice to have been contacted. We’ve been on this community for months and have repeatedly been asking if anyone was interested in joining us. In any case, we are about to put out the finite-sample theory and asymptotics of the linear model, and have already made the Lindeberg CLT public. Does this overlap with anything you’re doing/ asking for?

@Patrick Rubin-Delanchy Thank you so much for your message. It will be great and important to coordinate going forward. I will be happy to discuss more over Zoom to come up with a plan. We have provided an initial roadmap that is guiding the first set of projects on the page. Look forward to learning more from you.

Many thanks for proposing a call, I will message you directly about this.

In this thread, I will just keep to points that I think could matter to the community as a whole.

The announcement talks of open discussion and shared design decisions. What are the planned mechanisms for this, in particular to:
a) avoid unknowingly duplicating each other's work
b) make it easy for existing contributors and newcomers to find and join efforts
c) hold these discussions (e.g. email, zoom, workshops, zulip?)

The projects page asks anyone wanting to propose a new project to contact Rajarshi Mukherjee by email, while the contribute page suggests starting a discussion on the Statlib Zulip channel, which at the moment seems to be a single topic here under Project announcements. What are your thoughts on creating a dedicated channel, where people can say what they intend to work on and where architecture can be discussed in the open, to keep coordination visible to everyone rather than running through private email?
4 messages were moved here from #Project announcements > Statlib by Floris van Doorn.

Exciting! I’m curious what will set Statlib apart from Mathlib. Though I’m neither a mathematician nor a statistician, I don’t see why theorems and definitions in statistics would need to find a separate home from Mathlib. For instance, the expected value of a probability mass function is already in Mathlib - if someone builds on this, would their work belong in Mathlib or in Statlib?

Another question: will the foundations for statistics, probability, random numbers still go through measure theory (and inherited from Mathlib), or is an alternative being considered?

For me (not one of the statlib founders), there are pros and cons. Principal con (just my opinion): it could work against a deeper unification of maths and stats, which was a big reason I was drawn to this whole formalisation idea (as a statistician); Principal pro: more freedom to do things in a stats-friendly way. For example I remember hearing some people here suggesting to _remove_ matrices from Mathlib. Didn’t happen (and I’m not sure if it was a joke), but that would really have been disastrous for stats.
Maybe a dumb question: Is there a link to the actual GitHub repo for the project somewhere? The contribution page suggests there is one but I can't find it.
The link exists in https://stat-lib.github.io/tutorial/Installation-and-Setup/#Statlib--Installation-and-Setup and seems to be the only such link on the website

Oh I thought you were asking whether the website has the link and not what the link is;
in general for any X.github.io link you can find the repo at github.com/X
If that were the case, wouldn't it be https://github.com/stat-lib ? I need to know the repo name in addition to the org name right?
Yeah but that's usually trivial, their repo is right there at the link you sent

In retrospect it makes sense that whatever org was used to create the pages site would also host the Lean repo itself.

I guess that it would be nice if the pages site https://stat-lib.github.io/index.html had more direct links to the repo throughout so I have opened a PR to add them, hopefully the maintainers won't mind.
Thanks for the PR, it is very helpful!Really appreciate and I have merged it.

I m confused - checked this repo (https://statlean.github.io/website/) recently, which is also related to statistics in lean but seems heavily AI generated. Some discussion on the difference between Statlib and other isolated repos like this would be useful. Specifically, how would Statlib be responsible about its content and code with AI?

Hi @Álvaro Morales

Thanks a lot for opening this discussion. We have taken a close look at the repo (the repo has been updated in the last few hours since the question was posted, so I will focus on the initial content but will pay attention to incorporated changes), and there are some major differences that can be described in terms of purpose, content, choices, and community. 

Purpose: The main purpose of Statlib and many other functional open-source libraries is continuity and usability. The specific results that go into the library require choices regarding its level of abstraction and generality to support both further additions without substantive changes to the current content and downstream translation into usable results. This requirement often differs from a particular textbook and set of lecture notes, and, as a result, formalizing a given textbook, irrespective of the choice and level of AI use, does not serve the same purpose as a library.  As a specific example, suppose one is interested in incorporating a robust version of semiparametric efficiency theory—one of the repository's main initial components. Whereas the repo in question, since it deals with a single textbook, offers a lower-bound theory of efficiency for Euclidean space-valued objects targeting standard $\sqrt{n}$-rates of inference. While for the purpose of a particular textbook it allows a concise exposition of a topic through a specific subclass of examples, an actual theory of semi/nonparametric efficiency is much broader and allows for (i) more general target functionals (e.g., Banach space valued) and (ii) beyond $\sqrt{n}$-theory. These aspects of efficiency theory are not merely ornamental but are crucial to important results, such as the statistical efficiency of empirical distributions in nonparametric settings, going beyond i.i.d. data models, and tackling dependent data efficiency theories. However, a Euclidean-valued efficiency-theory proof of Local Asymptotic Minimaxity or the Convolution Theorem does not allow one to build such generalities on top of it. The fact that these considerations take a community effort and regular discussions on an open forum to eventually decide the architecture, vocabulary, abstraction, and content that populates a library is clear from the several prominent ongoing Lean 4 projects dedicated to contributing to Mathlib. Statlib is guided by a similar philosophy -- we have dedicated projects guided by community discussions held on the Statlib channel to precisely resolve these crucial aspects of library membership.

Content: Going beyond purpose and focusing purely on content and the consistency of source material might help us better understand the responsible use of AI, rigorous code review, and documentation for clarity. Textbooks make choices on specific versions of a result to include and thereafter often detail the proof of a particular subcase of a result to illustrate the main principles. However, the full details of a result can be relegated to references and other materials for the sake of compactness. However, for the sake of inclusion in a library, one needs to pay special attention to these before claiming that a particular result has been formalized and can be used for downstream purposes. As a specific example, once again focusing on efficiency theory for the sake of continuity with the previous point, the proof of the Local Asymptotic Minimax Theorem in the source material, for clarity, relies on additional assumptions of tightness and structure of the loss function. However, even for Euclidean functionals, a proof under these assumptions does not furnish a complete Local Asymptotic Minimax lower bound that is necessary to appeal to in future work. It is worth noting that the repository includes discussions on this. However, one needs to navigate each code contribution manually through the repo to understand these subtle choices, thereby complicating the systematic development of a subject area. 

Choices: Finally, it is worthwhile to focus on the choices one needs to make while using agentic coding and AI-driven formalization of a source material without community-agreed decisions. As is not uncommon for formalization efforts in Mathlib, certain edits are needed in the form of results to be included in a library first (see, e.g., the ongoing project on Brownian Motion). However, choices of such changes and edits, for the purpose of a library, are driven by an open-source consensus to guide future usability and development. An initial pass through the repo revealed the following examples of choices that differ from the source, but it remains unclear how they can serve the library's fundamental purpose, principle, and philosophy without open-source discourse and discussion.  First, the formalization of Theorem 8.11 (see attached pic), the parametric local asymptotic minimax theorem, differs from the textbook statement. The Lean file aims for a result that applies to every estimator sequence, but the actual proof of the theorem assumes uniform tightness of the $\sqrt{n}$-normalized estimator sequence, lower semicontinuity of the loss, a density/PDF infrastructure, and additional measurability or regularity hypotheses.  The book, for the sake of readability and exposition, states the theorem for any estimator sequence and introduces tightness and lower semicontinuity only in the proof, with a footnote noting that the general case follows from a compactification argument. Even if these are mentioned in the repo, it becomes increasingly daunting to keep track of such differences. Second, the semiparametric local asymptotic minimax theorem (Theorem 25.21) also warrants discussion. The source material states the theorem for a convex tangent cone, any estimator sequence, and subconvex loss, but Lean code effectively seems to linearize the tangent structure (i.e., work with a tangent space), and also assumes tightness of the estimator sequence (suitably scaled) to build on the parametric theory that assumes it.  Moreover, several later estimator or upper-bound theorems, for example, Theorem 25.54 (see attached pic), 25.57, and 25.77, are formalized under bundled asymptotic linearity hypotheses, rather than deriving those asymptotic linearity conclusions from first principles. 

Community: Last but not least is the question of community—the overused word in the discussions above. The duty and responsibility of a library is to serve the goals and future of a research community. Statlib, building on the philosophical and functional infrastructure of Mathlib, is dedicated to developing its content not only through open-source discussions but also through rigorous code review of every contribution. We describe these principles in detail at https://stat-lib.github.io/contribute.html, and our goal is to rigorously review every code contribution to ensure it mirrors Mathlib-level coding practices, abstraction, continuity, and usability. Compared to isolated repositories, this takes time to painstakingly develop every line of code, aligning with fundamental philosophies of usable, continuous research. Indeed, there are now multiple repositories, each claiming aspects of the same content. Without a platform for the group to come together and pursue future communal goals, it will remain unclear how to grow as an academic society that produces usable, formalized research.

We thank everyone for joining this space for these discussions and helping us build a community. We will add more discussions on this in the future.
